lessons.title: 01 · From symmetry actions to groups
lessons.summary: Understand the four group axioms and distinguish group order, element order and generators.
objectives: Explain the four group axioms through operation composition
Distinguish  group order  from the order of an operation
Understand the common fixed point of a point group

sections.title: Symmetry preserves the entire object
paragraphs: A rotation is a symmetry operation only if every chemically identical position, direction, and internal label coincides with its original counterpart afterward. Coloring one square corner breaks symmetries that move it to another corner. Crystal analysis must likewise retain chemical species rather than checking coordinates alone.

Every operation in a point group fixes the same point. Choosing it as the origin allows r′ = Rr with an orthogonal matrix R. Rotations, reflections, inversion and their combinations are allowed, but nonzero pure translations are not.

sections.title: Four rules constrain composite operations
paragraphs: Closure: composing two operations stays within the set. Associativity: changing brackets does not change the composition. Identity E changes nothing. An inverse completely undoes an operation. These rules do not require commutativity, so generally AB ≠ BA.

This course uses column vectors and active operations: AB means apply B first and then A. The inverse of a quarter-turn is a quarter-turn in the opposite direction, not the negative of every matrix entry.

sections.title: Count operations, not just axes
paragraphs: The  group order  |G| counts distinct operations. The order of operation A is the smallest positive integer n for which Aⁿ = E. A fourfold axis provides E, C₄, C₄², and C₄³; C₄² itself has order only 2.

Generators are a set of operations sufficient to produce the whole group. Repeated multiplication must supply every element. A list containing only E and C₄ is not a complete group, because C₄² and C₄³ are missing.

example.title: Generate C₄ using a 90° rotation
steps: Rotating (1,0,0) counterclockwise by 90° about z gives (0,1,0).
Continue rotating to obtain (−1,0,0) and (0,−1,0), returning to the starting point on the fourth turn.
The distinct operations are E, R, R², R³; multiplication simplifies using R⁴ = E.
For example, R³R² = R⁵ = R; R has inverse R³.
example.result: The group has order 4; R has order 4 and R² has order 2. This rotation subgroup is not the complete three-dimensional point group of an unmarked square.

lessons.pitfall: One symmetry axis can supply several operations. Composition has an order: matrices act from right to left.

quiz.question: Why is {E, R}, with R a 90° rotation, not yet a group?
choices: There is no rotation axis
R² is outside the set, violating closure
A group cannot contain the identity
quiz.explanation: Composing R with itself gives a 180° rotation, neither E nor R. Only after adding R² and R³ do we obtain C₄.

quiz.question: What is the order of the 180° rotation R² in C₄?
quiz.explanation: Two successive 180° rotations give the identity. The  group order  4 differs from this operation's order 2.

lessons.title: 02 · Understanding rotations, mirrors and inversion
lessons.summary: Understand Schönflies and Hermann–Mauguin notation through coordinate transformations.
objectives: Identify Cₙ, m, i, and  rotoinversion
Distinguish Sₙ from n̄
Read 4mm, 4/m, and 422

sections.title: Identify operations from coordinates
paragraphs: C₂(z) maps (x,y,z) to (−x,−y,z); a mirror perpendicular to z gives (x,y,−z); inversion i gives (−x,−y,−z). Reflection and inversion are different operations.

In an orthonormal Cartesian basis, RᵀR = I. Proper rotations have det R = +1; improper operations such as mirrors and inversion have det R = −1. The determinant indicates whether spatial handedness is reversed but does not uniquely identify the operation.

sections.title: Sₙ and n̄ combine different actions
paragraphs: Schönflies Sₙ means a rotation by 2π/n followed by reflection across the plane perpendicular to its axis, σₕCₙ. International n̄ means the same-angle rotation followed by inversion, iCₙ. They are generally not the same operation. In this website's text, −n denotes overlined n̄; the minus sign does not mean a negative rotation angle.

2̄ = iC₂ is the mirror perpendicular to the axis, written m. For the same oriented axis, 4̄ and S₄ are inverse operations but generate the same four-element group. Thus the international group name −4 corresponds to the Schönflies name S₄. Corresponding group names do not imply identical directions for their basic operations.

sections.title: Read the relative orientations of axes and planes
paragraphs: Cₙᵥ adds vertical mirror planes containing the principal axis; Cₙₕ adds a horizontal mirror perpendicular to it; Dₙ also includes twofold axes perpendicular to the principal axis. h,v,d are defined relative to the specified principal axis, not the screen's horizontal and vertical directions.

The two m symbols in 4mm denote two inequivalent sets of vertical mirrors. The slash in 4/m means that the mirror normal is parallel to the axis, so the mirror is perpendicular to it. 422 has a principal fourfold axis and two sets of perpendicular twofold axes. Cubic groups use different direction conventions and should be read together with operation matrices.

example.title: Why does multiplying C₂ by the perpendicular mirror give inversion?
steps: First apply m⊥z to (x,y,z), obtaining (x,y,−z).
Apply C₂(z) next to obtain (−x,−y,−z).
Reversing the order gives the same coordinates; these two particular operations commute.
They generate {E,C₂,m,i}, the group 2/m (C₂h).
example.result: 2/m necessarily contains inversion. By contrast, mm2 (C₂v), generated by C₂ and a mirror containing its axis, has no inversion.

lessons.pitfall: “Having improper operations” does not mean “having an inversion center.” −4（S₄） contains det R = −1 operations but not i alone.

quiz.question: Which operation maps (x,y,z) → (x,y,−z)?
choices: Inversion i
C₂(z)
Mirror perpendicular to z
quiz.explanation: It fixes every point in the xy plane; inversion reverses all three coordinates.

quiz.question: What correctly distinguishes 4mm from 4/m?
choices: 4mm has vertical mirrors; 4/m has a mirror perpendicular to the principal axis
Two notations for the same group
4/m has no fourfold rotation
quiz.explanation: They are C₄v and C₄h. Both have  group order  8, but their geometric actions differ.

references.chapter: §3.9–3.11, the two notations and symmetry operations

lessons.title: 03 · Why exactly 32 classes?
lessons.summary: Start from the crystallographic restriction and organize all ordinary crystallographic point groups by the seven crystal systems.
objectives: Understand permitted rotation orders
Locate the 32 point-group classes in seven crystal systems
Distinguish the meanings of 32, 14, and 230

sections.title: Periodicity restricts rotation orders
paragraphs: A rotation mapping a three-dimensional periodic lattice to itself is an integer matrix in a primitive lattice basis, so its trace is an integer. In Cartesian coordinates, an axial rotation by θ has eigenvalues 1,eⁱθ,e⁻ⁱθ and trace 1+2cosθ. Trace is basis-independent, so 2cosθ can only be −2,−1,0,1,2.

Finite-order rotations therefore allow only axes of order 1, 2, 3, 4, or 6. Requiring closure of combinations with mirrors and inversion, and classifying their three-dimensional geometric actions, gives 32 types. The restriction concerns three-dimensional periodic lattices; fivefold symmetry in isolated molecules and quasicrystals is consistent with it.

sections.title: Triclinic, monoclinic, orthorhombic: 2 + 3 + 3
paragraphs: Triclinic: 1 (C₁), −1 (Cᵢ). Monoclinic: 2 (C₂), m (Cₛ), 2/m (C₂h). Orthorhombic: 222 (D₂), mm2 (C₂v), mmm (D₂h).

This course uses common international short symbols, with −n replacing an overlined n. In mm2 with the twofold axis along z, the mirrors are xz and yz. Changing axes can give 2mm or m2m while retaining geometric type C₂v, but operation matrices and basis functions must transform with the coordinates.

sections.title: Tetragonal, trigonal, hexagonal: 7 + 5 + 7
paragraphs: Tetragonal: 4 (C₄), −4 (S₄), 4/m (C₄h), 422 (D₄), 4mm (C₄v), −42m (D₂d), 4/mmm (D₄h).
Trigonal: 3 (C₃), −3 (C₃ᵢ, also S₆), 32 (D₃), 3m (C₃v), −3m (D₃d). Trigonal names a crystal system; rhombohedral describes a related lattice or cell setting and is not fully synonymous.

Hexagonal: 6（C₆）, −6（C₃h）, 6/m（C₆h）, 622（D₆）, 6mm（C₆v）, −6m2（D₃h）, 6/mmm（D₆h）. −6m2 and −62m, and −42m and −4m2, are differently oriented symbols of the same respective geometric types; fixed lattice coordinates still require their orientation differences to be retained.

sections.title: The five cubic classes, and the distinction between 32 and 230
paragraphs: Cubic: 23 (T), m−3 (Tₕ), 432 (O), −43m (Tᵈ), m−3m (Oₕ). All have four threefold axes rather than a unique principal axis, and orders 12, 24, 24, 24, 48 respectively. The total is 2+3+3+7+5+7+5 = 32.

14 counts Bravais-lattice types; 230 counts three-dimensional ordinary  space group  types.  space group  additionally include lattice translations,  screw axis , and  glide plane . Quotienting a  space group  G by its pure-translation  normal subgroup  T gives G/T isomorphic to the crystal  point group . The 32  point group  cannot replace  space group  for a complete structure description.

Centrosymmetry, proper-rotation-only symmetry and polarity are different properties. Polarity requires a nonzero invariant polar vector. Having only proper rotations means that no operation reverses handedness, but does not imply polarity; 222 is an example.

example.title: All have fourfold axes: why do 4, 4mm, and 4/mmm differ?
steps: 4 contains only rotations about the principal axis, four operations in total, and permits an invariant polar vector along z.
4mm adds vertical mirrors for a total of eight operations; a polar vector along z remains invariant.
4/mmm includes a horizontal mirror and the associated composite operations, giving 16 operations and inversion symmetry.
A horizontal mirror reverses a polar vector along z, so 4/mmm permits no nonzero invariant polar vector.
example.result: The highest rotation order is only a starting clue; mirrors, transverse twofold axes and inversion must also be checked.

lessons.pitfall: 32 counts geometric types, not all finite point groups or abstract group isomorphism types. C₂, Cₛ, and Cᵢ are all abstractly isomorphic to the cyclic group of order two, but act differently in space.

quiz.question: Does a fivefold axis in a regular pentagonal molecule violate the crystallographic restriction?
choices: It violates the restriction; molecules cannot have fivefold axes
No contradiction: the restriction applies to three-dimensional periodic lattices
Only relabeling it a tenfold axis avoids a violation
quiz.explanation: Point symmetries of a finite molecule need not map a three-dimensional translation lattice to itself.

quiz.question: If two crystals both belong to m−3m, must their space groups be identical?
choices: Yes;  point group  retains all translations
Yes; cubic symmetry has only one space group
No; the point group omits full translation and nonsymmorphic information
quiz.explanation: Different combinations of lattices,  screw axis , and  glide plane  can have the same  point group  type.

lessons.title: 04 · From geometric symmetry to matrices
lessons.summary: Representations describe how physical quantities transform; conjugacy classes and characters make matrix information easier to compare.
objectives: Check representations by preservation of multiplication
Understand irreducible representations and common invariant subspaces
Read conjugacy classes, dimensions, and characters

sections.title: One group can act on different spaces
paragraphs: Spatial operations may act on positions, orbitals, displacements or spins. The object and chosen basis functions specify a matrix representation D(g). A group encodes multiplication of operations; a representation realizes it on a particular linear space. Representations need not be faithful: distinct group elements may map to the same matrix.

The matrices must preserve group multiplication. A basis change sends every matrix simultaneously to S⁻¹D(g)S and gives an equivalent representation. Incompatible bases cannot be chosen separately for individual operations.

sections.title: Blocks that cannot be simultaneously split further
paragraphs: A representation is reducible if one basis makes every group matrix share the same block structure. Finite-group representations over the complex numbers decompose into direct sums of irreducible representations. Representation dimension counts basis functions, not group operations.

In C₄v, the polar-vector space splits into the one-dimensional z space and the two-dimensional (x,y) space. Every group operation preserves both subspaces, corresponding to A₁ and E, so the vector representation is A₁ ⊕ E. E as a representation name differs from the identity operation; context distinguishes them.

sections.title: Read  character  by  conjugacy class
paragraphs: If h = xgx⁻¹, then g and h lie in the same conjugacy class. This can be viewed as moving an operation's axis or plane to an equivalent position using an allowed group transformation. Equal rotation angles or operation types do not guarantee conjugacy: the axial vertical mirrors and diagonal mirrors of C₄v lie in different classes.

The character χ(g) is the trace of D(g), constant within a conjugacy class and independent of basis. Each character-table column usually represents a class; numbers such as 2, 3, and 6 in headings are class sizes and must enter calculations. The identity character χ(E) = d gives the representation dimension.

example.title: character  of a three-dimensional polar vector in C₄v
steps: Use the order E,2C₄,C₂,2σᵥ,2σᵈ. The identity matrix has trace 3.
A 90° rotation has trace 1 and a 180° rotation trace −1. A mirror has two +1 eigenvalues and one −1 eigenvalue, giving trace 1.
Thus χᵥ = (3,1,−1,1,1). z belongs to A₁, with characters (1,1,1,1,1).
Subtracting the two rows gives (2,0,−2,0,0), the two-dimensional E representation carried by (x,y).
example.result: A three-dimensional vector need not form a three-dimensional irreducible representation: in C₄v it splits into one-dimensional A₁ and two-dimensional E.

lessons.pitfall: A  character  column gives the trace of each operation in that class, not the sum of traces over the class. Some textbooks combine a pair of one-dimensional  complex conjugation  representations into  real representation . The number of combined rows must not be mistaken for the number of complex  irreducible representation .

quiz.question: An irreducible representation has character 2 at the identity. What does this imply?
choices: The group has only two operations
This is a two-dimensional representation
The group must contain inversion
quiz.explanation: The identity is represented by a d×d identity matrix with trace d; this does not directly give the group order.

quiz.question: How should the basis change when testing reducibility?
choices: One basis change simultaneously block-diagonalizes every operation
Choose any basis separately for each operation
Diagonalize only one matrix
quiz.explanation: A common invariant subspace must be preserved by every group element; diagonalizing one matrix is insufficient.

lessons.title: 05 · Decompose representations using characters
lessons.summary: Reduce C₂v by hand and check integrality and dimensions.
objectives: Use conjugacy-class sizes as weights correctly
Distinguish direct sums from tensor products
Check  multiplicity  and dimensions

sections.title: Reduction is a weighted inner product
paragraphs: Let h be the group order, n꜀ the size of class c, χ the character to decompose, and χᵅ the character of irreducible representation α. Their inner product, weighted by class sizes and divided by h, gives the multiplicity aᵅ. The star denotes complex conjugation.

For an ordinary finite group,  complex representation  should yield nonnegative integer  multiplicity . Clearly negative or noninteger results usually indicate errors in column order, class sizes, operation conventions, or inputs; rounding must not conceal them.
sections.formula: aᵅ = (1/h) Σ꜀ n꜀ χᵅ(C꜀)* χ(C꜀)；Γ = ⊕ᵅ aᵅΓᵅ

sections.title: Fix the axes and column order of C₂v
paragraphs: Take the twofold axis along z and columns E, C₂(z), σ(xz), σ(yz); every class has size 1. The four irreducible representations are A₁: (1,1,1,1), A₂: (1,1,−1,−1), B₁: (1,−1,1,−1), B₂: (1,−1,−1,1).

Thus z belongs to A₁, x to B₁, y to B₂, and xy to A₂. Exchanging x and y exchanges the physical basis functions of B₁ and B₂. Align operations before comparing character tables, rather than comparing names alone.

sections.title: Add characters for direct sums; multiply them for tensor products
paragraphs: Placing two subspaces side by side gives a direct sum, whose characters add componentwise. Combining two objects, such as a product of functions, uses a tensor product: multiply characters componentwise and then reduce.

Decomposed dimensions must satisfy d = Σᵅ aᵅdᵅ. For the complete inequivalent complex  irreducible representation , squared dimensions sum to  group order  and their count equals the number of  conjugacy class . These checks apply to the same ordinary finite group.
sections.formula: χ(A ⊕ B) = χ(A)+χ(B)；χ(A ⊗ B) = χ(A)χ(B)；Σᵅ(dᵅ)² = h

example.title: Decompose the polar-vector representation of C₂v
steps: Coordinate matrices give χᵥ = (3,−1,1,1), with group order h = 4.
The dimension is 1+1+1 = 3; reconstructing characters entry by entry also recovers (3,−1,1,1).
example.result: Γᵥ = A₁ ⊕ B₁ ⊕ B₂, corresponding to z,x,y. This decomposes a vector space; it is not yet a count of vibrational modes for a particular structure.

lessons.pitfall: For an operation-by-operation list, sum over every operation directly. Multiply by class sizes only for a class-compressed list. Missing or double-counting weights gives incorrect results.

quiz.question: C₄v has class sizes 1,2,1,2,2. What is the reduction-formula denominator?
choices: 5, equal to the number of classes
8, equal to the number of operations
4, the highest rotation order
quiz.explanation: The denominator is the group order 1+2+1+2+2 = 8. The number of classes determines the number of complex irreducible representations.

quiz.question: In this lesson's C₂v convention, what is B₁ ⊗ B₂?
choices: A₁
B₁
A₂
quiz.explanation: Entrywise character multiplication gives (1,1,−1,−1), namely A₂, also corresponding to x·y = xy.

lessons.title: 06 · Find basis functions with projection operators
lessons.summary: Go from representation multiplicities to explicit functions, extracting symmetry components by weighted averaging.
objectives: Explain character projection
Construct polynomial basis functions for C₂v
Understand zero projection and normalization

sections.title: Filter out the target symmetry
paragraphs: The reduction formula gives multiplicities, not basis functions directly. A projection operator applies each group operation to a trial function and sums with target-character weights. The target component is reinforced while other components cancel by orthogonality.

The scalar-function convention is T(g)f(r) = f(Rg⁻¹r), preserving T(g)T(h) = T(gh). A character projector extracts all components of type α; it does not automatically select a particular partner in a multidimensional representation or distinguish repeated copies.

sections.title: Totally symmetric projection is a group average
paragraphs: All characters of the totally symmetric one-dimensional representation are 1, so its projector averages every transformed function. In C₂v, averages of x,y,xy vanish, while z,x²,y²,z² remain unchanged.

A zero projection means only that the trial function lacks the target component, not that the group lacks that representation. Try another function or start from a complete set of orbitals, displacements, or polynomials.

sections.title: Verification is still required after projection
paragraphs: For nonzero results, apply the generators to verify transformation laws, then normalize using the specified inner product. Several trial functions may produce linearly dependent results; remove duplicates and orthogonalize when needed.

The chosen basis-function space must be closed under the group action. For example, after choosing one atom's x displacement, include displacements of all other atoms and directions generated by operations, or degrees of freedom will be lost.

example.title: Extract four components from f = x+y+z+xy
steps: In order E,C₂,σ(xz),σ(yz), the transformed functions are x+y+z+xy, −x−y+z+xy, x−y+z−xy, −x+y+z−xy.
Average with A₁ weights (1,1,1,1) to obtain z.
Average with A₂ weights (1,1,−1,−1) to obtain xy.
Weights B₁=(1,−1,1,−1) give x; weights B₂=(1,−1,−1,1) give y.
The four results add back to the original function.
example.result: The four projections are z, xy, x, y. These basis functions are unnormalized; normalization requires a separately specified inner product.

lessons.pitfall: A character projector does not guarantee a unique, normalized and complete basis. Higher-dimensional representations allow partner freedom; repeated representations also allow mixing among copies.

quiz.question: What does a zero A₁ projection of x in C₂v mean?
choices: A₁ does not exist
The projection must be wrong
x has no A₁ component
quiz.explanation: x belongs to B₁; using z or x² instead gives a nonzero A₁ component.

quiz.question: What does character projection of a multidimensional representation usually give directly?
choices: The component in the subspace of that symmetry type
All partners, uniquely defined and normalized
Actual vibrational frequencies
quiz.explanation: Partners, multiplicity copies, and normalization require further treatment; frequencies also require dynamical information.

lessons.title: 07 · Read physical constraints from  point group
lessons.summary: Use polar vectors, axial vectors and quadratic functions to understand polarity and infrared/Raman selection rules.
objectives: Distinguish polar and axial vectors
Determine whether symmetry permits  polarity
Distinguish symmetry permission from actual modes and intensities

sections.title: Position and angular momentum transform differently
paragraphs: Displacements,  electric dipole  moments, and electric fields are polar vectors transforming as v′ = Rv. Angular momenta and magnetic moments are axial vectors transforming as a′ = det(R)Ra; the extra sign arises from the cross product of two polar vectors.

Inversion reverses a polar vector but preserves an axial vector. An xy mirror reverses the z component of a polar vector, but reverses the x and y components of an axial vector while preserving its z component. The atlas lists these two representations separately; they are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Polarity requires a vector invariant under the whole group
paragraphs: A uniform polarization P preserving  point group  G must satisfy RP = P for every operation. The 10 classes permitting nonzero solutions are 1,2, m, mm2,3,3m,4,4mm,6,6mm. m permits any direction within its mirror plane; 1 imposes no directional restriction.

This is a permission condition, not proof of nonzero polarization or reversibility by an external field. A polar point group alone does not establish ferroelectricity. Likewise, an axial vector allowed by an ordinary point group does not establish ferromagnetism: time reversal, magnetic groups and actual magnetic order must also be considered.

sections.title: IR probes linear coordinates; ordinary Raman probes quadratic coordinates
paragraphs: Under the  electric dipole  and harmonic approximations, IR-allowed vibrational types from the totally symmetric vibrational ground state occur in the polar vector (x, y, z). The symmetric polarizability tensor for ordinary nonresonant first-order Raman scattering transforms as x², y², z², xy, xz, yz.

For a general matrix element ⟨f|O|i⟩ not to be forced to zero by symmetry, Γ_f* ⊗ Γ_O ⊗ Γ_i must contain the totally symmetric representation. The conjugation symbol cannot be dropped arbitrarily because characters need not be real. Even an allowed matrix element may vanish for other physical reasons.

With inversion, the electric dipole has odd parity and ordinary Raman quadratic coordinates have even parity. Thus a vibrational mode of definite parity cannot have both first-order activities. But even parity alone does not ensure Raman activity, nor odd parity IR activity; the actual representation and polarization matter. Modes of different parity can also accidentally share a frequency.
sections.formula: IR: Γᵥ; Raman: Sym²(Γᵥ); Γ_f* ⊗ Γ_O ⊗ Γ_i ⊃ A_(totally symmetric)

sections.title: Actual mode counts require atom and displacement information
paragraphs: Character tables list allowed symmetry types only. For an isolated nonlinear N-atom molecule, subtract three translational and three rotational degrees of freedom from the 3N displacement representation; a linear molecule has only two independent rotations to subtract.

A three-dimensional crystal with N atoms per primitive cell has 3N phonon branches at Γ, including three acoustic branches; overall rotations must not be subtracted as for molecules. Frequencies, intensities, and eigenvectors require force constants and dipole or polarizability derivatives. An IR-allowed character-table type need not occur among a specific structure's optical vibrations.

example.title: Fix coordinates and derive the three water-molecule vibrations
steps: Place the molecule in the xz plane, choose z as the twofold axis, and order columns E,C₂,σ(xz),σ(yz). The atomic-position permutation characters are (3,1,3,1).
Multiply by the polar-vector characters (3,−1,1,1) to obtain the nine-dimensional displacement characters (9,−1,3,1).
Subtract translations A₁+B₁+B₂ and rotations A₂+B₁+B₂ to obtain vibrational Γ = 2A₁+B₁, of dimension 3.
A₁ has a z-like electric dipole and quadratic Raman tensors; B₁ has an x-like electric dipole and an xz-like Raman tensor. All three modes are therefore symmetry-allowed in both IR and Raman.
example.result: The two A₁ modes are symmetric stretching and bending; B₁ is antisymmetric stretching. Exchanging x and y often changes the notation to 2A₁+B₂ without changing the physical modes. Frequencies and intensities are not calculated here.

lessons.pitfall: “Allowed” does not guarantee existence, observability, or nonzero intensity. Ordinary  point group  omit  time reversal ; magnetic moments and magneto-optical questions additionally require magnetic groups.

quiz.question: How does angular momentum L transform under spatial inversion alone?
choices: L → −L, just like displacement
L is unchanged because it is an axial vector
L must vanish
quiz.explanation: L = r×p: inversion reverses both r and p, leaving their cross product unchanged. Time reversal is a different operation.

quiz.question: Does a Raman-allowed label directly determine peak intensity?
choices: Yes; intensity equals the representation dimension
Yes; all allowed peaks have equal intensity
No; modes, polarizability derivatives, and polarization are also required
quiz.explanation: Symmetry states only that coupling is not forbidden; it does not supply the modes, frequencies or coupling strengths of an actual structure.

lessons.title: 08 · From the classroom to the computation workbench
lessons.summary: Connect  point group , BC cells, k  little group , and standard labels, and recognize when  double group  and  magnetic corepresentation  are needed.
objectives: Distinguish the crystal point group, site-symmetry group and little group of k
Retain translation phases away from Γ
Choose tools according to spin and  time reversal

sections.title: Three kinds of groups in the same crystal
paragraphs: The crystal point group consists of the linear parts of space-group operations and is isomorphic to the quotient by pure translations. A site-symmetry group retains only operations fixing an atomic position and can be much smaller. Bands or phonons at wave vector k use the little group that preserves k modulo a reciprocal-lattice vector.

In the same  fractional coordinates  convention, x′ = Rx+t corresponds to k′ = R⁻ᵀk.  little group  requires R⁻ᵀk−k to have integer  reciprocal lattice -vector coordinates. At Γ with k = 0, every point operation qualifies; generic k usually retains fewer operations.
sections.formula: Gₖ = { {R|t} ∈ G : R⁻ᵀk = k+K }, where K has integer reciprocal-lattice coordinates

sections.title: Why ordinary point-group tables are insufficient
paragraphs: A Seitz operation {R|t} includes translation. Composing two operations can differ from another representative by a lattice vector even if their linear parts agree. This contributes a phase to Bloch states and cannot be discarded arbitrarily.

With active translations T(t)ψ(r) = ψ(r−t) and fractional reciprocal coordinates, the translation phase is exp(−2πik·t). It equals 1 at Γ, but nonsymmorphic space groups may require projective representations with a factor system at other k points. Point-group tables therefore cannot generally replace the space-group workbench.

sections.title: A reproducible learning path
paragraphs: First select a group in the 32- point group  atlas and inspect its operation count,  generator ,  conjugacy class , and geometric actions. Then reduce vectors by hand and compare with the atlas's polar-vector, axial-vector, and quadratic-function results. If they disagree, check coordinate bases and operation order first.

For a real crystal, open Structure → BC cell, import POSCAR/CIF and check elements, identification tolerance, space group and transformations. Use the converted cell and k in the representation workbench, then inspect BC/Bilbao labels. Origin, basis, operation representatives and spin gauge may all affect matching; unmatched labels must not be filled in by guessing names.

sections.title: Extend further for spin or magnetism
paragraphs: Spinless displacements and ordinary scalar orbitals normally use  single-valued representation . Half-integer-spin spinors change sign under 2π rotation and require consistent  double group  bookkeeping. Double-valued does not mean simply duplicating every ordinary representation.

Time reversal is antiunitary. Magnetic groups and corepresentations require explicit complex conjugation and magnetic-structure information. This classroom and atlas focus on ordinary spatial point groups; further questions belong in the double-valued representation and magnetic-corepresentation modules, within their stated coverage.

example.title: Check C₄v at the Γ point of P4mm
steps: Select 4mm (C₄v) in the atlas. Its order is 8 and irreducible dimensions are 1,1,1,1,2, whose squares sum to 8.
In the ordinary space-group workbench, choose No.99, P4mm, single-valued representations, and Γ=(0,0,0). This symmorphic space group has translation phase 1 at Γ and can be checked against C₄v.
Align characters using operation matrices or  conjugacy class . Do not assume local software labels D1, D2 have the same order as textbook A₁, A₂.
Change k to (0.137,0.219,0.071) and observe the reduced little group at a generic point; do not continue to apply the full C₄v table directly.
example.result: Point groups provide geometric and algebraic foundations; actual bands and phonons also require space groups, wave vectors, and translation phases.

lessons.pitfall: Cell standardization changes more than a title. Real-space bases, origins, and reciprocal k must transform together; k in an input cell cannot simply be treated as BC-cell coordinates.

quiz.question: Why are the 32 point-group tables generally insufficient for representations away from Γ?
choices: Non-Γ points have no symmetry
Translation phases and  nonsymmorphic  operations affect representation multiplication
Point groups apply only to molecules
quiz.explanation: First select the k little group and retain translation phases; nonsymmorphic space groups can also have nontrivial factor systems.

quiz.question: How are 2π and 4π rotations represented for half-integer spin?
choices: They must all equal +I
2π gives +I and 4π gives −I
2π gives −I; 4π returns to +I
quiz.explanation: A spinor changes sign under a 2π rotation and returns after 4π; this is why double groups are introduced.
